I use on of two joysticks when I'm emulating the Astrocade under MAME:
1) Atari 2600 controller (CX40) with the original Stelladapter.  This adapter hasn't been sold since, I think, 2009, but you can read about the specs and build you own here:
http://www.grandideastudio.com/stelladaptor-2600/

There is also the 2600-dapter, which does pretty-much the same thing, but works with FAR more controllers.   I own this adapter too-- I just don't use it that often.  The 2600-dapter can be bought here:
http://www.2600-daptor.com/

2) Ideally, if you want a "true" Bally Arcade/Astrocade experience (or as close as you can get with MAME's emulation of the hardware), then you can use an Astrocade controller with the Astro-daptor:
http://www.2600-daptor.com/Astro-daptor.htm

The Astro-daptor works really well with both modes of the Astrocade hand controller: the knob (i.e. "paddle") and the eight-direction "joystick."  The Astro-dapter can be purchased here:
http://www.2600-daptor.com/Astro-daptor.htm
When running Astrocade emulation, I prefer the 2600 controller-- but it won't work for any games that require the knob to be used at the same time (for example, GUN FIGHT).

Adam

The Bally maps out all inputs through SENTRY. The only reason I can think of it not working is that you may have a bad cell in one of your memory chips. That would cause possible erratic behavior of the SENTRY latch. The RWB Utility will NOT check the 4000h region of memory. You may need to do a program that checks all bits (or bytes) of screen ram. DO NOT CHECK THE STACK AREA as it will crash the program and maybe mess up something you may have in expanded memory.
I can write you a program in either BASIC or machine language that will do a thorough check of each bit under various conditions.
Of course you could have a bad I/O, ROM, ADDRESS, or DATA chip causing this condition, also.

As far as GA not pausing, that could be that they mapped it out in their SENTRY setup.
Ken

The Multi-program system actually runs like a cart. It is controlled by the cartridge slot hardware. When you select the Ulti, it shifts it to the 2Kh area, so it runs like a Multicart. You just don't have the dip switches to change from one game to another. It will all be done through the MENU selection process of the On Board ROM. The Bally maps out all inputs through SENTRY. The only reason I can think of it not working is that you may have a bad cell in one of your memory chips. That would cause possible erratic behavior of the SENTRY latch. The RWB Utility will NOT check the 4000h region of memory. You may need to do a program that checks all bits (or bytes) of screen ram. DO NOT CHECK THE STACK AREA as it will crash the program and maybe mess up something you may have in expanded memory.I can write you a program in either BASIC or machine language that will do a thorough check of each bit under various conditions.Of course you could have a bad I/O, ROM, ADDRESS, or DATA chip causing this condition, also.
As far as GA not pausing, that could be that they mapped it out in their SENTRY setup.Ken

I've been disassembling the 280 Zzzap/Dodgem game for the Astrocade.  The game is only 2K, so I thought that it might be fun to look at how it works.  The game isn't among my favorites for the Bally Arcade console-- in fact, it's not that fun to play (it's too easy).  However, it's simple and I figured that I might learn something while disassembling it.  Plus, the home version was programmed by Jay Fenton.  Jay also programmed the original arcade version of the game.  That version uses an 8080 CPU rather than the Bally Arcade's Z80 CPU, but otherwise the game's are very similar.


If you can't remember what 280-Zzzap looks like, then imagine the Atari 2600 game Night Driver.  It's a front-on view of you looking out the windshield of your car while driving down a (very) twisty road at night, with only the road's signposts to guide your way.  I've never seen or played the arcade version of 280-Zzzap, but I became interested in the game due to it's relationship to the Astrocade.


I found a video of someone playing the arcade version of 280-Zzzap. The video is low quality, but it gives a really good example of just how much of the game is missing when played in MAME.  The arcade game looks pretty damn sweet compared to the Astrocade version.  Not only is the resolution higher (although it's limited to only black and white), but the arcade game used mirrors (or some such "magic") to give a background to the game (like, I think, was done with Space Invaders).  The game also makes great use of screen overlays and it has some nifty sounds.  I imagine these sounds, like many early arcade games, can't be emulated properly in MAME.  That's probably why MAME's version of 280-ZZap is missing all sound effects.: the game plays totally silently under emulation-- which is a shame.

Here is the video of the actual arcade game in action:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EPJBCOiVDrg
[https://www.bing.com/th?id=OVP.V752ff3c23cecd2d9a496ba37b94591fa&pid=Api]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EPJBCOiVDrg>

www.youtube.com
1976 Midway 280Zzzap arcade game (The steering pot is flaky...that's why I'm pretty much all over the road)



I had planned to use the Astrocade controller (with the Astro-dapter USB adapter) to play 280-Zzzap in MAME, but the arcade game requires more inputs than the Astrocade version of the game.  For instance, in the arcade game you have to shift between low and high gears (no shifting is required in the home port of the game).


Here's how the controls break down for use:


Shift (High/Low) - Digital button

Accelerator (Gas pedal) - Analog

Steering Wheel - Analog


I ended up using my Logitech Rumblepad 2 controller (which is similar to the Playstation 2 controller) to play the game in MAME.  This gamepad just doesn't feel at all natural compared to the Astrocade's hand controller's knob-- or, imagine, the arcade game's setup.

What do other people think of this game?  Does anyone enjoy playing Z80 Zzzap / Dodgem now, or have fond memories of playing the game (either in the arcade or on the Astrocade)?

Adam

The BASIC bonus game for this round's Astrocade High Score Club is WaveMaker's Outpost 19.  It is a pretty amazing game for little 'ol "AstroBASIC."  I find myself strangely infatuated with it; I have already spent several hours playing it today.  The transporters, which are absolutely required to escape the alien, are invisible (and therefore difficult to find).  That's a shame; they should have been marked in each room for the player.  As it is, you have to stumble across the transporters by searching each room carefully.  Luckily, the transporters are always in the same location.  If they were randomly placed, the game would be too difficult to play.



Today, I made a map of Outpost 19 in Photoshop.  The map contains the location of each of the eight transporters (marked in green), plus the destination (marked in red).  The map was a cinch to make using the skills that I honed a few years ago creating The Temple of Apshai Trilogy maps in Photoshop.  Well, it was a cinch to make the map... but it did take quite a bit of time to create it.  I've attach the map to this post.


I wish that I had a color printer to print this map out-- it's useful in B&W... but it would be much easier to use in color.  Maybe I'll get it printed at a copy store.



Adam

    I've been disassembling the 280 Zzzap/Dodgem game for the Astrocade.  The game is only 2K, so I thought that it might be fun to look at how it works.  The game isn't among my favorites for the Bally Arcade console-- in fact, it's not that fun to play (it's too easy).  However, it's simple and I figured that I might learn something while disassembling it.  Plus, the home version was programmed by Jay Fenton.  Jay also programmed the original arcade version of the game.  That version uses an 8080 CPU rather than the Bally Arcade's Z80 CPU, but otherwise the game's are very similar.
If you can't remember what 280-Zzzap looks like, then imagine the Atari 2600 gameNight Driver.  It's a front-on view of you looking out the windshield of your car while driving down a (very) twisty road at night, with only the road's signposts to guide your way.  I've never seen or played the arcade version of280-Zzzap, but I became interested in the game due to it's relationship to the Astrocade.

I found a video of someone playing the arcade version of 280-Zzzap. The video is low quality, but it gives a really good example of just how much of the game is missing when played in MAME.  The arcade game looks pretty damn sweet compared to the Astrocade version.  Not only is the resolution higher (although it's limited to only black and white), but the arcade game used mirrors (or some such "magic") to give a background to the game (like, I think, was done with Space Invaders).  The game also makes great use of screen overlays and it has some nifty sounds.  I imagine these sounds, like many early arcade games, can't be emulated properly in MAME.  That's probably why MAME's version of280-ZZap is missing all sound effects.: the game plays totally silently under emulation-- which is a shame.

Here is the video of the actual arcade game in action:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EPJBCOiVDrg
|   | Midway 280-Zzzapwww.youtube.com1976 Midway 280Zzzap arcade game (The steering pot is flaky...that's why I'm pretty much all over the road) |


I had planned to use the Astrocade controller (with the Astro-dapter USB adapter) to play280-Zzzap in MAME, but the arcade game requires more inputs than the Astrocade version of the game.  For instance, in the arcade game you have to shift between low and high gears (no shifting is required in the home port of the game).
Here's how the controls break down for use:
Shift (High/Low) - Digital button
Accelerator (Gas pedal) - AnalogSteering Wheel - Analog

I ended up using my Logitech Rumblepad 2 controller (which is similar to the Playstation 2 controller) to play the game in MAME.  This gamepad just doesn't feel at all natural compared to the Astrocade's hand controller's knob-- or, imagine, the arcade game's setup.

What do other people think of this game?  Does anyone enjoy playing Z80 Zzzap / Dodgem now, or have fond memories of playing the game (either in the arcade or on the Astrocade)?

Adam

The BASIC bonus game for this round's Astrocade High Score Club is WaveMaker's Outpost 19.  It is a pretty amazing game for little 'ol "AstroBASIC."  I find myself strangely infatuated with it; I have already spent several hours playing it today.  The transporters, which are absolutely required to escape the alien, are invisible (and therefore difficult to find).  That's a shame; they should have been marked in each room for the player.  As it is, you have to stumble across the transporters by searching each room carefully.  Luckily, the transporters are always in the same location.  If they were randomly placed, the game would be too difficult to play.

Today, I made a map of Outpost 19 in Photoshop.  The map contains the location of each of the eight transporters (marked in green), plus the destination (marked in red).  The map was a cinch to make using the skills that I honed a few years ago creating The Temple of Apshai Trilogy maps in Photoshop.  Well, it was a cinch to make the map... but it did take quite a bit of time to create it.  I've attach the map to this post.

I wish that I had a color printer to print this map out-- it's useful in B&W... but it would be much easier to use in color.  Maybe I'll get it printed at a copy store.

Adam

    I've been disassembling the 280 Zzzap/Dodgem game for the Astrocade.  The game is only 2K, so I thought that it might be fun to look at how it works.  The game isn't among my favorites for the Bally Arcade console-- in fact, it's not that fun to play (it's too easy).  However, it's simple and I figured that I might learn something while disassembling it.  Plus, the home version was programmed by Jay Fenton.  Jay also programmed the original arcade version of the game.  That version uses an 8080 CPU rather than the Bally Arcade's Z80 CPU, but otherwise the game's are very similar.
If you can't remember what 280-Zzzap looks like, then imagine the Atari 2600 gameNight Driver.  It's a front-on view of you looking out the windshield of your car while driving down a (very) twisty road at night, with only the road's signposts to guide your way.  I've never seen or played the arcade version of280-Zzzap, but I became interested in the game due to it's relationship to the Astrocade.

I found a video of someone playing the arcade version of 280-Zzzap. The video is low quality, but it gives a really good example of just how much of the game is missing when played in MAME.  The arcade game looks pretty damn sweet compared to the Astrocade version.  Not only is the resolution higher (although it's limited to only black and white), but the arcade game used mirrors (or some such "magic") to give a background to the game (like, I think, was done with Space Invaders).  The game also makes great use of screen overlays and it has some nifty sounds.  I imagine these sounds, like many early arcade games, can't be emulated properly in MAME.  That's probably why MAME's version of280-ZZap is missing all sound effects.: the game plays totally silently under emulation-- which is a shame.

Here is the video of the actual arcade game in action:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EPJBCOiVDrg
|   | Midway 280-Zzzapwww.youtube.com1976 Midway 280Zzzap arcade game (The steering pot is flaky...that's why I'm pretty much all over the road) |


I had planned to use the Astrocade controller (with the Astro-dapter USB adapter) to play280-Zzzap in MAME, but the arcade game requires more inputs than the Astrocade version of the game.  For instance, in the arcade game you have to shift between low and high gears (no shifting is required in the home port of the game).
Here's how the controls break down for use:
Shift (High/Low) - Digital button
Accelerator (Gas pedal) - AnalogSteering Wheel - Analog

I ended up using my Logitech Rumblepad 2 controller (which is similar to the Playstation 2 controller) to play the game in MAME.  This gamepad just doesn't feel at all natural compared to the Astrocade's hand controller's knob-- or, imagine, the arcade game's setup.

What do other people think of this game?  Does anyone enjoy playing Z80 Zzzap / Dodgem now, or have fond memories of playing the game (either in the arcade or on the Astrocade)?

14778:
I added the BALLY BASIC version of THE PITS by Rex Goulding.  This was published in ARCADIAN 3, no. 10 (Aug. 12, 1981): 108.

The "AstroBASIC" version of THE PITS was archived by Paul Thacker on October
30, 2005.  Today, I loaded THE PITS into "AstroBASIC."  I then saved it to the BALLY BASIC 300-baud format using the Dave Ibach cartridge conversion method.  This conversion method isn't foolproof (it requires that you swap "AstroBASIC" for the BALLY BASIC cartridge while the system is turned on), but it worked for me today (the second time that I tried it).

I compared THE PITS' program code to the ARCADIAN BASIC listing.  I realized that there were a few (minor) changes.  I made the BALLY BASIC version match exactly with the game as originally printed in the newsletter.  This entailed adding a few ending quote marks, changing the loop length in lines 640 and 680 and NOT typing in line 720 (which should be an unnumbered line).  I also added the program comments from lines 1-4 back into the program.

The game now plays a little slower (not really a bad thing, in this case) and the sound effects work correctly.  I didn't even realize that they sounded "off" in the "AstroBASIC" version before today.  I actually think this version of the game is slightly better than when it runs under "AstroBASIC."  I mean, it runs a bit smoother in "AstroBASIC" (which, I admit, is nice), but the game seems to be tuned for play under BALLY BASIC.  This makes perfect sense, because the game was probably published before "AstroBASIC" was released.

If you haven't played this game before, then why not try it now?

Adam

From an electronics design critique, that is the absolute WORST place to tie to. I could pick up and noise that is generated by anything on the entire PCB. If you use the "Ring" connector in the picture, you really should put it on the screw that is right next to the power supply connector. BE CAREFUL not to let it touch any of the components nearby!!!! If necessary, trim down the connector or place tape over the component leads. Next best place is right next to the on/off switch.Ken

14792:
I added ARCADE GOLF By Mike Maslowski.  This program is from CURSOR 1, no. 6 (July 1980): 42-45.  This program was typed in from the CURSOR newsletter by me on August 31, 2016.  It was archived using the 300-baud utilities TXT2PRG and KCSWIN.

This was easily one of the most time-consuming programs I've ever archived.  Partially, it is because the program is long.  Also, it takes three programs to finally create the final one-load BASIC program.  For this reason, there will be no "AstroBASIC" version of this program available.  While it may be possible to create it-- it wouldn't be an easy fix.

Finally, making sure that they program had no errors took some time.  Luckily, once I got the hang of how to play this version of ARCADE GOLF, it was an okay game to play.  I wouldn't pass-up THE INCREDIBLE WIZARD to play this game, but it's fun enough.  My only issue with it is that you can't aim your ball with precision.  It's a weird mechanic, but you do get (sort of) used to it.  I mean, you can aim your ball, but it's a strange method that requires marking your controller to "calibrate it" (see the instructions, below) on how set up your controller.

Note that this version of ARCADE GOLF is NOT related to Ken Lill's golf game of the same name.  All they share in common is the name ARCADE GOLF.  Ken's game is actually based on Bob Hensel's game GOLF.  Both of these other GOLF games are superior to this one... but there had to be a first golf game on the Bally Arcade, and this version of ARCADE GOLF is it.

IMPORTANT: The ARCADE GOLF archive contains four different programs, but only one program is actually required to run the program in Bally BASIC.  The program that you RUN is called:

Arcade Golf (Main Program and Initialization) (1980)(Mike Maslowski)(300-Baud)

The other three programs were required to create the final executable version of ARCADE GOLF (above).  For archive purposes, those three programs are also included in the archive:

Arcade Golf - Initialization (1980)(Mike Maslowski)(300-Baud)
Arcade Golf (1980)(Mike Maslowski)(300-Baud).wav
Arcade Golf Variables (300-Baud)

You can download ARCADE GOLF here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/cursor/cursor.html#ArcadeGolfMikeMaslowskiBB


One aspect of the CURSOR/THE BASIC EXPRESS newsletters that I've always like is the considerable effort put into programs documentation.  ARCADE GOLF is one of the best documented BASIC programs published.  I've OCRed/retyped the full documentation, which is included here:


Editor's Note [From CURSOR]:

This is one of the most innovative programs that we have seen written for Ballys' 2K.  This game utilizes graphics; allows you to select from 14 clubs, has doglegs, water hazards, sand traps, roughs, wind effect, and penalties.  If you play golf, this program is a must!  If you don't, this program will turn you into a "hacker" in no time at all.

Play Instructions:

Golf is a one to four player game lasting 1-99 holes (selectable).  Each hole will be different.  Start with just a few holes until you get the hang of it.

All Players Use Hand Controller #1

To start the match, enter the number of golfers and number of holes to be played.  You will then be asked how hard you want the course layout to be.  One (1) is the easiest and ten (10) the most difficult.  The higher the number you enter, the higher the probability of sand traps and doglegs.  The last question asked is the average wind speed for the day. The harder the wind is blowing, the more it will affect the flight of your shots, particularly on hits.  Until you get the hang of the game, it's best to set wind speed to zero (0).

Before playing golf for the first time, hand control #1 must be calibrated.  This can be done by keying in this one line calibration program prior to loading the ARCADE GOLF program.

10 PRINT KN(1);GOTO 10

Adjust the knob for zero and mark this position so that the knob is lined up with the trigger (zero position points to trigger).  You can draw a small line or arrow on the top of the knob to do this.  A small arrow or line from a dry transfer set does a nice permanent and professional looking job.

To select a club, pull back on the joystick and turn the knob until the proper club appears on the screen (see chart of clubs and ranges).  To gauge the force of your swing, move the joystick forward and turn the knob until the desired force (0-4) is displayed.  Zero is the low end of the clubs' range, and 4 is the high end.

After club and force are selected, set direction of the hit by turning the knob with the joystick in its' neutral position.  When the arrow on the top of the knob is pointing at the trigger, the ball will go straight (towards the right of the screen).  To angle the ball left (toward top of screen), turn the knob to the left; to angle right (toward bottom of screen), turn the knob to the right.  The direction will vary from straight towards the right of the screen to straight up (left) or straight down (right).  You cannot hit backwards.

Note: The entire working range of the knob is about 1/4 turn, therefore even very small changes in the knob position affect direction.

Penalty Strokes:

If your ball travels off the fairway there is a one stroke penalty for hitting from the rough.  Over the green, and running the entire width of the fairway, is a lake.  If you hit in the lake, the ball will be dropped in front of the green and a one stroke penalty is added.

Once you get on the green, your turn is over.  You will have 2, 1 or 0 putts added to your stroke total, depending on whether you landed somewhere on the green, very close to the hole, or in the hole.  Pull back on stick to set up next hole.

New Game: Press "GO" on keypad to start a new game.

Club                 Range

P = Putter             8 - 24
C = Chipper           26 - 42
S = Sand Iron         44 - 60
W = Wedge             62 - 78
9 = 9 Iron            80 - 96
8 = 8 Iron            98 - 114
7 = 7 Iron           116 - 132
6 = 6 Iron           134 - 140
5 = 5 Iron           152 - 168
4 = 4 Iron           170 - 186
3 = 3 Iron           188 - 204
2 = 2 Iron           206 - 222
F = Fairway Wood     224 - 240
D = Driver           242 - 258

Golf Initialization Statement Program

To squeeze all of ARCADE GOLF into 1800 bytes, array elements and screen colors are initialized using immediate instructions (no line numbers).  To get these instructions stored on tape, a small program (the Golf Initialization Statement Program) was written.  This program writes initialization statements to tape when "GO" is pressed.

Until ARCADE GOLF is running properly, it is wise to store the initialization statements on a separate tape.  The separate tape MUST be loaded AFTER Arcade Golf and also following any changes to the ARCADE GOLF program.  The reload is required after changes because array locations are dependent on program size (array values are unpredictable when program size changes).

Once ARCADE GOLF is keyed in correctly, record the initialization statements immediately following Arcade Golf.

Program Documentation

     10 Initialize game variables
     20 Input game parameters
     50 Increments hole # & checks for
        End of Game
 55- 65 Load hole variables w/new configuration
        using RND numbers
100-130 Generate hole graphics for all P1
SWING ROUTINE:
    150 Loops through CLUB/FORCE/WIND
        subroutine unti1 TR(1)
    155 Length of hit calculated from club
        & force var. Angle of hit determined
        by KN position
    160 Trig subrt. called to determine XY
        co-ordinates of shot
165-170 Check penalties. N=1 for ball in
        rough, N=2 in lake, N=3 in sand. If
        ball in letter graphics, move to
        fairway edge; in lake, ball is
        dropped in front of green.
    172 Check for ball on green.
    179 Draw flight of ball, display any
        penalty message (sub590+N) add to
        stroke count of ball not on green
    180 If ball not on green, go to SWING
ON GREEN:
185-190 Calculate # of putts based on
        distance from hole
    195 Display strokes and putts for hole
    200 Update total stroke counters
    205 Wait until joystick off center
    210 If last player, GOTO NEW HOLE rout.
    215 More players, GOTO Gen.hole Graph.
CLUB/FORCE/WIND Subroutine
    500 If joystick forward, convert KN
        value to force 0-4 & update screen
    505 If joystick back, convert KN value
        to club 0-13 & update screen (l is
        added to club var. to correspond
        to array elements 1-14).
    510 Calculate wind speed within 5MPH
        of average originally input.
    515 Display wind speed
COSINE TRIG Subroutine
    530 Angle is passed in var. Z. 2 digit
        cosine resulting from cosine
        approximation calculation is ret. in Z.
STROKE COUNT Subroutine
    560 Update stroke count
    570 Display new stroke count
SAND TRAP Subroutine
    580 Displays Sand Trap on Left or
        Right side of green depending on
        Value in I.
PENALTY MESSAGE Subroutine (590+N)
    590 N=0 Shot OK CLEAR previous statement.
    591 N=1 Rough
    592 N=2 Lake
    593 N=3 Sand
    594 N=4 On green, just return

Variable Index

A = Length of hole 100-565 yards
B = Number of players 1-4
C = Club Selection 0-13
D = Left Sand Trap flag, if on trap is created
E = Right Sand Trap flag, if on trap is created
F = Force of swing 0-soft to 4-hard
G = Current hole number
H = Total number of holes to be played
I = Work variable, used as loop counter and for par passing
J = Y co-ordinate of tee
K = Angle of hit 0 degree-90 degree
L = Length of hit
M = Difficulty factor 0-easiest 10-hardest
N = Work variable, used as loop counter, storage
    of temporary values i.e., +/- direction
    penalty message number
O = Par for current hole

P = Current player number 1-4

Q = X co-ordinate of hole
R = Y co-ordinate of hole
S = Current stroke count
T = Number of puts
U = Dogleg flag, if on dogleg is created
V = X direction size of dogleg rough
W = Current wind speed
X = X co-ordinate of ball
Y = Y co-ordinate of ball
Z = Work variable used to hold temporary values
    and pass parms to subrtn (i.e., passes
    angle to co-size subrtn which rtns 2 digit
    cosine in Z)

@(1) - @(14) = An ASCII representation of club selection (see chart).
@(15)- @(18) = Total scores for players 1-4
       @(19) = Average wind speed
       @(20) = Wind direction
       @(21) = Total par

Note: After loading, GOLF, requires SZ=43 to run (21 array elements x2)+I.  If you don't have that many bytes left, you have not copied the program exactly as we have printed it, go back and check for errors!!!


Have fun!


Adam

Before playing golf for the first time, hand control #1 must be calibrated.  This can be done by keying in this one line calibration program prior to loading the ARCADE GOLF program.

10 PRINT KN(1);GOTO 10

Adjust the knob for zero and mark this position so that the knob is lined up with the trigger (zero position points to trigger).  You can draw a small line or arrow on the top of the knob to do this.  A small arrow or line from a dry transfer set does a nice permanent and professional looking job.

To select a club, pull back on the joystick and turn the knob until the proper club appears on the screen (see chart of clubs and ranges).  To gauge the force of your swing, move the joystick forward and turn the knob until the desired force (0-4) is displayed.  Zero is the low end of the clubs' range, and 4 is the high end.

After club and force are selected, set direction of the hit by turning the knob with the joystick in its' neutral position.  When the arrow on the top of the knob is pointing at the trigger, the ball will go straight (towards the right of the screen).  To angle the ball left (toward top of screen), turn the knob to the left; to angle right (toward bottom of screen), turn the knob to the right.  The direction will vary from straight towards the right of the screen to straight up (left) or straight down (right).  You cannot hit backwards.

Note: The entire working range of the knob is about 1/4 turn, therefore even very small changes in the knob position affect direction.

Penalty Strokes:

If your ball travels off the fairway there is a one stroke penalty for hitting from the rough.  Over the green, and running the entire width of the fairway, is a lake.  If you hit in the lake, the ball will be dropped in front of the green and a one stroke penalty is added.

Once you get on the green, your turn is over.  You will have 2, 1 or 0 putts added to your stroke total, depending on whether you landed somewhere on the green, very close to the hole, or in the hole.  Pull back on stick to set up next hole.

New Game: Press "GO" on keypad to start a new game.

Golf Initialization Statement Program

To squeeze all of ARCADE GOLF into 1800 bytes, array elements and screen colors are initialized using immediate instructions (no line numbers).  To get these instructions stored on tape, a small program (the Golf Initialization Statement Program) was written.  This program writes initialization statements to tape when "GO" is pressed.

Until ARCADE GOLF is running properly, it is wise to store the initialization statements on a separate tape.  The separate tape MUST be loaded AFTER Arcade Golf and also following any changes to the ARCADE GOLF program.  The reload is required after changes because array locations are dependent on program size (array values are unpredictable when program size changes).

Once ARCADE GOLF is keyed in correctly, record the initialization statements immediately following Arcade Golf.

14799:
When you save (dump) to tape (or PC) you have to remember that you are saving in the direction from the beginning of the program toward the end of space. So to save a *() array, you will need to know it's length (remember it is 2x the number of array elements +2. Now, you need to subtract that number from the end of program and then :PRINT %(xxxxx),nnnn where xxxxx = to the address of end- array length*2 +2more. nnnn is the number of bytes for the array.I hope you can understand this complicated way, but that is the only way I know to save just the *() array.Ken

I was at the Computer History Museum last week in Mountain View, CA.  I was most excited to see the Astrocade on display and posted a couple pictures in the yahoo group here:
 

 https://groups.yahoo.com/neo/groups/ballyalley/photos/albums/1143713594 https://groups.yahoo.com/neo/groups/ballyalley/photos/albums/1143713594

 

 I was disappointed that the blurb next to the display focused on its unfortunate market timing and neglected to mention all the great things about the Astrocade (unique pistol grip controllers, built in cartridge storage, keypad, 4-player capability, etc.) or the strong following that it has to this day.
 

 Here's the blurb next to it at the museum (shown in the photo):
 

 Astrocade Professional Arcade game console, Bally Technologies, US, 1977
 Dave Nutting designed a powerful graphics processor to pair with a Zilog Z80 microprocessor in this 1977 home game console.  Originally called the "Bally Home Library Computer," it was refocused on gaming applications just in time to fall victim to the 1983 video game market crash.  It was taken off the market in 1985.

This works fine.  Hopefully you're using the latest version of MAME (MESS isn't updated anymore).  MAME has "taken over" all the home consoles and computers.  I should probably update the Astrocade emulation area to reflect this reality.


>>

I've never heard anyone refer to Bally Alley as "the alley."  I like it!


>>

>>


These VERY brief instructions presume that you're using the latest release of MAME (which, right now, is mame0177).  They also presume that MAME is setup correctly and you've tested it by loading other cartridges.


To Setup MAME to run the Vipersoft BASIC cartridge:


1) Start MAME


2) Press Tab to get to the options.


3) Select "Slot Device"


4) Select a RAM expansion device (there are five choices).  Since you have a Lil' White Ram already, we'll use that hardware for this example: select "lil_white_ram."


5) Load the Vipersoft BASIC cartridge.  It's called "VIPERb.bin"


You're done!  Now you can write and run expanded BASIC programs.  Of course, you can't save your work.  Since you've already used AstroBASIC under emulation, then you're already familiar with this limitation.  Man, I wish saving and loading worked under emulation.  It would make arching program a breeze!


One interesting difference (besides the extra commands and smaller character set) between the two BASICs is the pressing the Reset button on the Astrocade will wipe out your memory in "AstroBASIC."  In Vipersoft BASIC, that's NOT the case: pressing Reset leaves your program intact (at least under emulation-- I can't remember if this works on real hardware).


Also, if you're using AstroBASIC emulation for BASIC, then hopefully you've printed a set of the BASIC overlays for a keyboard that I made back in 2011:


http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/MESS/mess.html#AstrocadeMESSBASICKeypadOverlay


I used these overlays to write the ultra simple example program that I used as an example screenshot of Vipersoft BASIC running in MAME.


Have fun programming!


Adam

A few days ago I created graph paper for the Astrocade BASIC screen layout of 160x88.  I figured that others might find it useful, so you can download it too:


http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/basic.html#AstrocadeBASICScreenLayoutGraphPaper

Here is a full explanation of the graph paper:

The resolution of Bally BASIC and "AstroBASIC" bitmap screens is 88x160. BASIC commands (such as BOX and LINE) layout the screen as a graph with the origin in the center of the screen with X ranging from -80 to 79 and Y ranging from -44 to 43. This graph paper was created to help layout this screen. The graph shows the Astrocade's full low-resolution 102x160 screen, including hexadecimal memory address locations. However, the black horizontal and vertical lines on the graph paper were created using the "AstroBASIC" LINE commands and show exactly the BASIC resolution of 88x160. A screenshot was taken using MAME and then superimposed over the graph paper. The black lines are laid-out every ten pixels starting from the origin.

The archive includes three versions of the graph paper: a jpg, a TIFF image (with layers), and a TIFF (with no layers, "flattened"). To make the best use of the TIFF files requires a graphics editor (such as Photoshop or GIMP) that can deal with layered TIFF files. With the layered TIFF image, a user can use Bally Arcade/Astrocade screenshots taken from the Astrocade emulator included with MAME to create screen layouts on "graph paper." These can then be used to help understand how an Astrocade program functions (such as how the screen is built or laid-out). Instructions explain how to combine a screenshot as a separate layer on the "graph paper."

The instructions on how to do this are available here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Screen%20Layout%20Graph%20Paper/Astrocade%20Screen%20Layout%20-%20102%20x%20160%20Graph%20Paper%20(Doc)(CR).txt

I hope that you find this graph paper useful!

Adam

Are the Bally joysticks wearing out your trigger finger?  Well, mine too!  But, there is a solution.  But, first, some background.


I recently bought a flash cartridge for my Sega Genesis called the Mega Everdrive.  The Genesis is software backward compatible with the Sega Master System (though the SMS cartridges won't fit into the Genesis cart slot without the Genesis Master System converter).  The Everdrive allows the user to play SMS games on the Genesis without that converter.  Cool!


Much to my surprise, I've actually found myself playing more SMS games than Genesis games.  I discovered that the Genesis 3-button controller works with most games-- but not all of them.  I don't have a SMS controller, so I converted a spare (broken) NES controller to work as a SMS controller.  It works great.


That got me to thinking.  What about using this SMS controller on the Astrocade?  I'd need an Atari to Astrocade adapter for that.  So, I started making on yesterday and finished it this morning.  A little while ago I played Cosmic Raiders using the converted NES controller (for the Sega Master System ) on the Astrocade using the Atari to Bally Astrocade joystick adapter.  It works great!


For more information on making an Atari joystick to Bally Astrocade adapter, read section 10 ("Joystick Rewiring (Bally/Atari)") in the Bally/Astrocade FAQ:


http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/bally-astrocade_faq.txt


With the adapter you can use an Atari compatible joystick.


I should have made this adapter a long time ago!


Adam

It's been a while since I've played Galactic Invasion, but assuming the scoring is like Galaxian, the biggest points are awarded for having a formation of 3 ships come at you with the yellow ship on top and hit the yellow ship first. Try taking out as many of the bottom row as possible without them peeling off and maxing your bonus score by waiting for the yellow ships to peel off before shooting them. Moving to the corners of the screen is a quick way to die. Try to stay as close to the center of the bottom as much as you can without getting hit.

I have added a partial disassembly of 280 Zzzap / Dodgem to BallyAlley.com.  This 2K cartridge, released in 1978 by Bally Mfg. Corp., contains two mediocre driving games.  The cartridge was programmed by Jay Fenton.

Remember, this is a preliminary Z80 disassembly of the 280 Zzzap / Dodgem cartridge.  This is the first release of this code.  It is very rough: some of the code has been disassembled and the car graphic pattern has been found, but most code is still not commented.


I'm not sure if I'll revisit this code again.  Since it's been lingering on my hard drive for a couple of months, I figured that it would be nice to share it with those that might be interested in this sort of techie thing.

Have fun!

14841:
UV-1/ZGRASS Video: "Nuke The Duke"
Published on YouTube by "videoman909" Jan 23, 2013.

This is probably the most sophisticated UV-1 video that I've ever seen.  While the graphics see dated, the message seems timeless.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0gBQtOodxTQ
[https://i.ytimg.com/vi/0gBQtOodxTQ/hqdefault.jpg]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0gBQtOodxTQ>

Nuke The Duke - YouTube<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0gBQtOodxTQ>
www.youtube.com
Independent video created by Charles Kesler and Jake Postma in 1983. Charles created the graphics on a Datamax UV-1 computer, which could use only 4 colors ...

Here is the video's description from YouTube:

"Independent video created by Charles Kesler and Jake Postma in 1983. Charles created the graphics on a Datamax UV-1 computer, which could use only 4 colors at a time, this video won 1st place and Best in Show at the London Intn'l Film Festival as well as awards in Chicago, New York and San Francisco film festivals.

"John Wayne (the Duke) died of cancer as did many other cast members of a film being shot near a nuclear test site, when the wind changed and blew over the film shoot.

This was the first of a trilogy of art videos that received acclaim around the world for drawing awareness to the Cold War and the stockpiling of nuclear weapons.  Winner of several international computer animation film festivals. It's also been on display at the NC Museum, of Art as well as many other museums and festivals around the world.

"Video images of John Wayne were kine-scoped from television sets and added to the graphics through a video switcher. The Datamax UV-1 was a pioneering computer designed by a group of computer graphics artists working at the University of Illinois at Chicago, known as the Circle Graphics Habitat. It was primarily the brainchild of Tom DeFanti, who was trying to build a machine capable of running his GRASS programming language at a personal computer price point, a project they referred to as the Z-Box.

"As time went on the project evolved into a machine intended to be used to make high-quality color graphics for output to videotape, and later as a titling system for use by cable television companies. This video was created on what seems to be the first dedicated graphics workstation."

It would be neat to talk to some of these people who used these UV-1 systems and programmed in ZGRASS!

"As time went on the project evolved into a machine intended to be used to make high-quality color graphics for output to videotape, and later as a titling system for use by cable television companies. This video was created on what seems to be the first dedicated graphics workstation."

It would be neat to talk to some of these people who used these UV-1 systems and programmed in ZGRASS!

Adam

I've used the 300 baud processing tools to digitally process a number of WaveMakers programs. These were previously only available as raw recordings. These are smaller and should load more reliably. Most programs now on-line come from the Mike Peace's master tapes. I've also sorted through whatever I could find from my backlog of recordings from these alternate sources--Brett Bilbrey's tape collection, Bob Fabris's tape collection, Jack Flynn's tape collection, and Ken Lill's tape collection. These did reveal alternate versions, including a version of Fortune Teller that doesn't crash like the version on the master tapes does.

We still need to test Whiz Quiz--that has a huge number of loads. I also have some tapes from Mike White I've never looked at, so there could be alternates on those. But these have been in progress too long already, so I'll go ahead and send Adam what I've got.

Here are my complete notes on the programs.

Backgammon (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Backgammon (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. The code differs in several places, but it's not immediately obvious that it plays differently.

Backgammon (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a2] - Found on commercial tape in Jack Flynn's tape collection. The main program is identical to the version from the master tapes, but the introduction program is slightly different.

Brick 'N The Wall (1982)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD) - found on hand-labeled tape in Bob Fabris's collection.

Clue (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Clue (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - archived from commercial tape in Jack Flynn's collection. Slightly different than version from master tapes.

Guitar Course Introduction (1980)(WaveMakers)(PD)[spoken] - This is a spoken introduction from Mike Peace found in Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It's addressed to George, perhaps George Moses.

Guitar Tuning & Guitar Course (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[Guitar Course tape side 1][From Master Tapes]

Guitar Tuning & Guitar Course (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[Guitar Course tape side 1][a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It's formatted differently and there are a few code differences, but it's not immediately obvious that it plays differently.

Horse Race (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Invasion Force (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Lookout For The Bull! II tape][From Master Tapes], Invasion Force (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Pack-Rat II tape][From Master Tapes] - The code in the two versions is slightly different.

Lookout For The Bull! (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Lookout For The Bull! II (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Max (Robot From Space) (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Mazemaker (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Flying Ace tape][From Master Tapes] - This is slightly different than the versions previously digitally archived.

Mazemaker (with introduction) (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It seems closest to "Mazemaker (with introduction) (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)", but has some formatting and code differences.

Mazemaker II (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Perversion tape][From Master Tapes]

Mazemaker II (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - found on tape in Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled "WaveMakers Extras - Natasia The Fortune Teller, Mazemaker II, Memory Doodle". The code is slightly different than the version from the master tapes.

Maze Race, Obstacle Course (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Memory Doodle (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD) - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. The comments describe it as a "no-charge extra". I didn't find a 300 baud version of this program on the master tapes. I also found a version of this on a tape in Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled "WaveMakers Extras - Natasia The Fortune Teller, Mazemaker II, Memory Doodle" which appears to be identical aside from archiving errors.

Mouse In The Hat (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Mouse In The Hat (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection.  It's a little different than the version from the master tapes, but it's mostly just formatting. However, it doesn't work correctly. You can never kill the mice. It's missing a direct setting of the variable P, so it may have been improperly copied.

Music Composer (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[with Oh Susanna][From Master Tapes] - To compose music, turn the knob to choose duration and push joystick up or down to move notes on scale. Push joystick right to place note, or pull trigger to place a rest. To go back to main menu, push joystick down until you're off the scale, then pull trigger.

Music Composer (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[with Oh Susanna][a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. There are both code and formatting differences from the version on the master tapes.

Music Composer (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[with The Man On The Flying Trapeze] - I created this file by combining two recordings from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection--"Music Composer (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[with Oh Susanna][a]" (with the music data removed) and "The Man On The Flying Trapeze (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[for Music Composer]". On the WaveMakers master tapes, I found a 2000 baud version of The Man On The Flying Trapeze, but no 300 baud version.

Note Match & Chord Progressions (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[Guitar Course tape side 2][From Master Tapes] - crashes with certain combinations. I checked another copy from Brett Bilbrey's collection, and the code is identical.

Obstacle Course Tournament (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Obstacle Course Tournament (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It's a little different than the version from the master tapes, but it's mostly just formatting.

Obstacle Course Tournament (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a2] - This is from a commercial tape in Jack Flynn's collection. It's slightly different than the other versions.

Pack-Rat (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Pack-Rat (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This version was found in Ken Lill's tape collection, and is slightly different than the version from the WaveMakers master tapes.

Pack-Rat II (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Perversion (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Pack-Rat II (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This version was found in both Brett Bilbrey's and Ken Lill's tape collections, and is slightly different than the version from the WaveMakers master tapes.

Sideswipe (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Horse Race and Yahtzee tapes][From Master Tapes] - identical versions were on both the Horse Race and Yahtzee master tapes

Sideswipe (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. The code is quite a bit different than the version from the master tapes.

Slot Machine (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Space Chase (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Speed Math, Note Match (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Tape 5 Introduction (1980)(WaveMakers)(PD)[spoken] - This is a spoken introduction from Mike Peace found in Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It's addressed to George, perhaps George Moses.

The Man On The Flying Trapeze (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[for Music Composer] - This is music data only for The Man On The Flying Trapeze for WaveMakers Music Composer program. I found it exactly like this in Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It must be combined with the Music Composer program to use. On the WaveMakers master tapes, I found a 2000 baud version of this song, but no 300 baud version.

WaveMakers Fortune Teller (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[Freebee with Space Chase][From Master Tapes]

WaveMakers Fortune Teller (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - found on tape in Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled "WaveMakers Extras - Natasia The Fortune Teller, Mazemaker II, Memory Doodle". Unlike the version from the master tapes, this doesn't crash when you ask for a second fortune.

WaveMakers Tapes Are (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Tape 5] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection, and seems to be from Tape 5. It's simply a promotional listing of the first six WaveMakers tapes.

Yahtzee (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Yahtzee (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It's a little different than the version from the master tapes, but it's mostly just formatting.

... The version of Sideswipe on Flynn's Clue tape was identical to Sideswipe (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Horse Race and Yahtzee tapes][From Master Tapes]

David Dibbern wrote:
>>
This is not a demodulator, it is a capture device.
>>

Understood.  I already have the demodulator from the same company.

>>
I really want a composite or a YUV output from my Astrocade, and I would think if you can get the svideo output, getting the composite out of that should not be too hard.  Isnt it the Y + U+V analog combined with sync on green?
>>

I have an s-video upgrade for my Astrocade, but it tends to ghost the TV image pretty badly, so I use the RF instead.  I'm not sure how the video signal of the Astrocade is made (that's tech I just don't even try to understand).

I think (but am not sure) that some versions of Ken's new Red White and Blue Ram expansion can have composite out.  I'm not sure if this feature made it into Ken's final version of the PCB.

For more information on composite-out (B&W only, I think), see the Astrocade FAQ (section 9, "Connecting a Monitor"):

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/bally-astrocade_faq.txt

Also, Michael Matte's hi-res Astrocade that he created in 1986 had color composite output.  Maybe you can glean how he did it from his instructions:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/hi-res_packages/hi-res_packages.html

I used to strive for the best picture possible for most of my older systems.  I've come to realize that the RF connection is how millions of people played these classic game systems (and computers) for twenty (or more) years.  I grew up with a Commodore 64 connected via RF to a 13" color TV.  It never bothered me.  I guess if it was good enough for us then, why isn't it good enough for us now?

These systems were designed actually look better with some color bleeding and blurring.  For instance, a couple of years ago, I hooked up my Atari 130XE (part of the 8-bit line) to my TV video using an s-video cable.  I soon realized that any games that created color by using artifacting showed up in B&W when using s-video.  I thought that there was a problem with my cable.  Nope.  It turns out that the video is just too clear and the trick that artifacting uses to achieve color on a normally B&W screen doesn't work unless you're using composite or RF connections. David Dibbern wrote:
>>

Sure, I can catch you up a little bit.  It seems you have some experience with using BASIC already, so that shouldn't be too difficult.

>>
I really , really want to play QB-2B.

Glad to hear it!  It's a pretty fun game-- but remember, it's written in BASIC, so it's limited compared to a game released on cartridge.  That doesn't mean a BASIC game can't be fun, but they probably shouldn't be judged on the same level.

>>
Bally basic was the original cart, with the 300baud external interface, right?
>>


Yes, Bally BASIC was the original cart with the external interface.  However, technically, the later version (with the built-in 2000-baud interface) was also released as Bally BASIC.  However, to differentiate it from the original BASIC cartridge release in 1978, most people call the 1981 release "AstroBASIC," "Astrovision BASIC," or (in the case of the Astrocade newsletters), sometimes, "New BASIC."

>>
Games were not directly interchangable [between 300-baud and 2000-baud BASIC], right?
>>


You are right; under normal circumstances you can't load 300-baud programs into "AstroBASIC."  You also can't load 2000-baud programs into Bally BASIC.  BallyAlley.com has most programs in AstroBASIC format, some programs in 300-baud format, and a few programs in both formats.  There are also some expansion RAM programs that require either Vipersoft BASIC or Blue Ram BASIC.

>>
Are there MP3's of the recordings from tape to D/L and then upload?
>>

There are over 500 programs that are available for download for BASIC.  Among these is QB-2B, a game that will only run under "AstroBASIC."  You can download QB-2B here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/wave_makers/QB-2B%20(WaveMakers).zip


To load a program, you can try a few different methods.  The method that works best for me is that I load the WAV file onto my old iPhone 5 and then load the song directly into "AstroBASIC."  Once the Astrocade program is on my phone, I do the following:


1) Plug one end of a 1/8" cord into my phone and the other end in the "AstroBASIC" cart.


2) In "AstroBASIC" type :INPUT;RUN and then press GO.


3) Now press play on the phone.  About twenty seconds later your program will be loaded and you'll be playing QB-2B (or any other program you choose to load).


When putting WAV files onto your phone, make sure that the file doesn't get compressed by iTunes.  I think you have to choose an option like "no compression" (or something similar to that.  Sorry, it has been awhile since I've adjusted my iTunes settings).

>>
Do I have to type it all in by hand?
>>


You don't have to type any BASIC programs by hand, as most of them are available in digitally archived format already.  However, if you have a young son or daughter, then you should certainly make them type in a very long BASIC program and carefully explain to them that it's for their own good.  When the program doesn't work due to careless syntax errors caused by typing mistakes (or, worse an error in the original printout!), then shrug your shoulders and say something comforting like, "Better luck next time!"  Many of us typed in programs when we were younger, they often had issues, and yet... we liked it, right?  Right?!?

Adam

I used to strive for the best picture possible for most of my older systems. Glad to hear it!  It's a pretty fun game-- but remember, it's written in BASIC, so it's limited compared to a game released on cartridge.  That doesn't mean a BASIC game can't be fun, but they probably shouldn't be judged on the same level.

>>
Bally basic was the original cart, with the 300baud external interface, right?
>>

Yes, Bally BASIC was the original cart with the external interface.  However, technically, the later version (with the built-in 2000-baud interface) was also released asBally BASIC.  However, to differentiate it from the original BASIC cartridge release in 1978, most people call the 1981 release "AstroBASIC," "Astrovision BASIC," or (in the case of the Astrocade newsletters), sometimes, "New BASIC."

>>
Games were not directly interchangable [between 300-baud and 2000-baud BASIC], right?
>>

You are right; under normal circumstances you can't load 300-baud programs into "AstroBASIC."  You also can't load 2000-baud programs into Bally BASIC.  BallyAlley.com has most programs in AstroBASIC format, some programs in 300-baud format, and a few programs in both formats.  There are also some expansion RAM programs that require eitherVipersoft BASIC or Blue Ram BASIC.

>>
Are there MP3's of the recordings from tape to D/L and then upload?
>>

There are over 500 programs that are available for download for BASIC.  Among these isQB-2B, a game that will only run under "AstroBASIC."  You can download QB-2B here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/wave_makers/QB-2B%20(WaveMakers).zip
To load a program, you can try a few different methods.  The method that works best for me is that I load the WAV file onto my old iPhone 5 and then load the song directly into "AstroBASIC."  Once the Astrocade program is on my phone, I do the following:
1) Plug one end of a 1/8" cord into my phone and the other end in the "AstroBASIC" cart.
2) In "AstroBASIC" type :INPUT;RUN and then press GO.
3) Now press play on the phone.  About twenty seconds later your program will be loaded and you'll be playingQB-2B (or any other program you choose to load).

When putting WAV files onto your phone, make sure that the file doesn't get compressed by iTunes.  I think you have to choose an option like "no compression" (or something similar to that.  Sorry, it has been awhile since I've adjusted my iTunes settings).

>>
Do I have to type it all in by hand?
>>

You don't have to type any BASIC programs by hand, as most of them are available in digitally archived format already.  However, if you have a young son or daughter, then you shouldcertainly make them type in a very long BASIC program and carefully explain to them that it's for their own good.  When the program doesn't work due to careless syntax errors caused by typing mistakes (or, worse an error in the original printout!), then shrug your shoulders and say something comforting like, "Better luck next time!"  Many of us typed in programs when we were younger, they often had issues, and yet... we liked it, right? Right?!?

Adam

I used to strive for the best picture possible for most of my older systems.  I've come to realize that the RF connection is how millions of people played these classic game systems (and computers) for twenty (or more) years.  I grew up with a Commodore 64 connected via RF to a 13" color TV.  It never bothered me.  I guess if it was good enough for us then, why isn't it good enough for us now?

These systems were designed actually look better with some color bleeding and blurring.  For instance, a couple of years ago, I hooked up my Atari 130XE (part of the 8-bit line) to my TV video using an s-video cable.  I soon realized that any games that created color by using artifacting showed up in B&W when using s-video.  I thought that there was a problem with my cable.  Nope.  It turns out that the video is just too clear and the trick that artifacting uses to achieve color on a normally B&W screen doesn't work unless you're using composite or RF connections.  This isn't to say that I wouldn't like the best picture possible on any system that I'm using, but I'd prefer RF to emulation or no picture at all.

Adam

>>
I really , really want to play QB-2B.
>>

Glad to hear it!  It's a pretty fun game-- but remember, it's written in BASIC, so it's limited compared to a game released on cartridge.  That doesn't mean a BASIC game can't be fun, but they probably shouldn't be judged on the same level.

>>
Bally basic was the original cart, with the 300baud external interface, right?
>>

Yes, Bally BASIC was the original cart with the external interface.  However, technically, the later version (with the built-in 2000-baud interface) was also released as Bally BASIC.  However, to differentiate it from the original BASIC cartridge release in 1978, most people call the 1981 release "AstroBASIC," "Astrovision BASIC," or (in the case of the Astrocade newsletters), sometimes, "New BASIC."

>>
Games were not directly interchangable [between 300-baud and 2000-baud BASIC], right?
>>

You are right; under normal circumstances you can't load 300-baud programs into "AstroBASIC."  You also can't load 2000-baud programs into Bally BASIC.  BallyAlley.com has most programs in AstroBASIC format, some programs in 300-baud format, and a few programs in both formats.  There are also some expansion RAM programs that require either Vipersoft BASIC or Blue Ram BASIC.

>>
Are there MP3's of the recordings from tape to D/L and then upload?
>>

There are over 500 programs that are available for download for BASIC.  Among these is QB-2B, a game that will only run under "AstroBASIC."  You can download QB-2B here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/wave_makers/QB-2B%20(WaveMakers).zip

To load a program, you can try a few different methods.  The method that works best for me is that I load the WAV file onto my old iPhone 5 and then load the song directly into "AstroBASIC."  Once the Astrocade program is on my phone, I do the following:

1) Plug one end of a 1/8" cord into my phone and the other end in the "AstroBASIC" cart.

2) In "AstroBASIC" type :INPUT;RUN and then press GO.

3) Now press play on the phone.  About twenty seconds later your program will be loaded and you'll be playing QB-2B (or any other program you choose to load).

When putting WAV files onto your phone, make sure that the file doesn't get compressed by iTunes.  I think you have to choose an option like "no compression" (or something similar to that.  Sorry, it has been awhile since I've adjusted my iTunes settings).

>>
Do I have to type it all in by hand?
>>

You don't have to type any BASIC programs by hand, as most of them are available in digitally archived format already.  However, if you have a young son or daughter, then you should certainly make them type in a very long BASIC program and carefully explain to them that it's for their own good.  When the program doesn't work due to careless syntax errors caused by typing mistakes (or, worse an error in the original printout!), then shrug your shoulders and say something comforting like, "Better luck next time!"  Many of us typed in programs when we were younger, they often had issues, and yet... we liked it, right?  Right?!?

Adam

14867:
The Rocket comes with a Component cable, which can be used as a composite cable if yellow goes into blue.  You can hook this up either to a computer or independent of a computer.   You can watch what your capturing via HDMI, with less than 1/60 second on HDMI input mode, and passes data in its original resolution, if it’s 480i, 480p, 720p, 1080i, or 1080p.  Low-definition progressives are upgraded to 480p, so it might cause a delay doing that.  Also my particular monitor, a Playstation  3D Monitor has 2 quirks.   One is it can’t do 480i or low-definttion progressives in HDMI mod without upgrading it to 480p, and the video automatically stretches 4x3 to 16x9, no matter what I do.  I think it’s just a display issue because a Xbox One HDMI input understands the 4x3 mode and compensates for it, and the Xbox composes a NEW 16x9 video based on the 4x3 video pillar boxed, but, as I’ll mention later, ping is horrible.

There are 2 usb plugs, one goes to the computer and one goes to a console or USB-to-Power supply.  It can be recorderd into a Flash dirve, and POSSIBLY (not sure) to a USB based full Hard Drive.  There is a 3.5 mm hole for commentary, but NOT the Xbox One Quad cord cable.  You need a 3-pole-to-43-pole 2.5 mm-to3.5 mm converted that you can find at Radio Shack.  NOT THE ONE on the Xbox One 2.5 to 3.5 converter, and if you use a Turtle Beach so similar surround product with an L/R or a 3.5 mm output with anything except an HDMI, you can reroute the surround sound into the L and R audio and it would be encoded in Dolby Headphone, and manual 3D video games which can have a left eye/right eye half width picture be recorded in side-by-side mode be viewed on a 3D TV with 3D playback.   I could upload a video showing it.  The videos are stored in MPEG-4 mode, it can be edited in IMovie, and can be played on a PS3 and Xbox 360 directly through the USB port, but not an Xbox One for some strange reason.

The reason why I split the RF signal is to get the lowest ping signal directly to a CRT TV, which is a requirement for light gun games.   If you’re going to do a game that requires low ping, if you split the video before the Rocket, sometimes the video will not process.   I found an S-Video booster you plug into the S-vdeo lead to the Rocket, and it corrects the signal and records properly.   I’m looking for something that can take an RCA and boost either composite or green component.  It’s hard to find one at either Radio Shack or Best Buy.  The only one I can find is an F-Type connector.    I know there are converters from F-Type to RCA and back, but I don’t know if the composite or black and white plus sync gets altered with a form altering.    If it doesn’t, I might want to buy 2 F-Type to RCA connectors and another 2 way RF splitter.    Also I am wondering if you need to power all 3 video ports in components of if one is good enough.   Hauppauge says the sync is a little flakey if split and not boosted.  This way I can get Time Crisis 2 in Component with a Guncon

But even if you don’t want to to boost the signal, you can use a Hauppauge in a wway where you don’t need a signal booster.  If the second video feed is plugged in a VCR or DVD recorder,  it boosts the signal before it goes into the Rocket because those devices run on electricity and the electricity boosts the signals.

And if you want to see what a performance enhancement a CRT TV and a direct connection does, look at my Bally High score on Astro Zap.   Starting around 25k points, almost everything is a nail biter.   This WAS played on a CRT TV, and split-routed through a DVD recorder, but I took the component video out and transferred it instantly to a Rocket.   Note to do well, DO NOT watch the footage from the Rocket. Watch the Direct CRT feed.  Here’s my high score video. I dare you to beat this score using a non-CRT TV.

Most  video DA’s amplify the composite signal.  the output is usually greater than the input.   If you just take a signal booster designed for RF , a coax booster, it boosts signals in the RF band, and the modulated signal.  changing the input will not always work, you need to check the frequency response of the splitter.
A standard RF splitter is a -3.5 db drop.  a 3 way is one @ -3.5 and 2 @ -7 db.  every split is -3.5 db

over or under driving a NTSC signal can have all sorts of problems. I will need to be highly technical here. If you don't understand waveforms as seen on an oscilloscope, then this info will be useless to you.
first, and foremost, any time you overdrive a signal in electronics, you run the chance of overshoot. to understand these effects more simply, take a guitar playing normally through an amplifier. When you overdrive the signal, it distorts the signal to give a "GRUFF" sound. It is sometimes called "FUZZ". It takes what is normally a sine wave and turns it into a modified square wave. The leading and trailing edges actually may be higher in voltage than the rest of the signal, causing "ringing" which is like the ghosting seen on TVs. It can also throw off the color burst signal that is responsible for the proper shift of color. that can change true blue to have either more green or red inserted, etc.The maximum voltage of the video signal above zero (what can be seen on the screen) is 0.7V for full brightness. The sync pulses are from zero to -0.3V (black to blacker than black) with the color burst capacitively coupled 0.3V (from 1.5V to -1.5V) within the vertical blanking pulse.Over driving this will cause color shift.
If you have a scope that is at LEAST 100MHz should show you these signals. If any of these signals have a spike on either the leading or trailing edges, then you are over driving your signal. If your square waves have spikes, you are over driving.That's about as simple as I can state it.To make sure your signal is good you need an oscilloscope and have knowledge of how to use it.
Ken

equipment to draw a set of color bars in the proper order it will make
referance points that are pre established on the NTSC vectorscope, or a
"ladder" on the wave form monitor. Notice on the pic of the NTSC
vectorscope how the color points are dead on?   Remember, this is for NTSC
Composite video... and for perfection.  If I were

a game I was good at, and set the value at 1 on the output of the amp and
record one min of the game, then record another minute of the game turning
it up by 1, and then visually comparing them to see what value gave me the
best picture., or I would write a quick basic program to make a set of
color bars and record them for 1 min, pause my recording device, adjust the
output by 1 and recodr another minute, and continue through all the output
values if the amp..  Kramer makes a good line of pro-sumer video processing

I’ll explain, I need to split a Componet video signal for my more modern system that uses a light gun.   If I wantt the best picture, I have to split a component signal, but because a Hauppauge Rocket is kind of finicky if the video is split using a standard unpowered Y-Cable.  I noticed with S-Video that I can split an S-Video signal if the route before entering the Rocket is power boosted, by plugging it into the power outlet as well as the input and output.  However, I’m having a tough time finding one for Composite and component RCA signals.  I know the Astrocade uses an RCA RF connector, you would normally plug that into a switchbox, and that leads out to the TV’s F-Type antenna port. The astrocade, I use a powered splitter, with 3 FType to RCA converters, and an F-Type cable for both  1 input and  2 outputs, and a power cord to strengthen the signal. I uploaded the photo of the PROM custom data chip mentioned a few posts back.  Ken Lill was the one to identify it based on my description.  The chip was from a spare Bally motherboard I had acquired in a collection of items from a former Bally employee.

I also posted some photos of various motherboards, each with slightly different revision or changes made. Per ipdb:
"The flyer refers to the "exclusive" Bally "Game Brain" circuit board. This is a different "Bally Brain" than the original Bally's 1974 'Flicker' prototype. A 1999 GameRoom magazine article indicated that David Nutting of David Nutting Associates signed an agreement with Midway in 1976 to produce home versions of pinball machines, using his company's "Bally Brain" invention.
The Bally Brain of the article was a 4004-based unit installed in a Flicker pinball. The Bally Brain of the Fireball/Galaxy Ranger/Evel Knievel/Captain Fantastic home professional series used a Fairchild F8 processor for series 1 and a Mostek 3870 for series 2 and is based on the architecture of the original Bally Brain."

14893:
I'm pretty sure the video anomalies are due to the capture device not
interpreting the source video correctly, which can happen with
"non-standard" signals from older hardware. For instance, with the Atari
2600, this can manifest itself as not capturing all of the ghosts in
Pac-Man because of the technique used to display all of the ghosts in the
game. It's quite common, actually.

I personally get around these legacy video issues for all eras of systems
and all worldwide video formats by putting everything through an XRGB-mini
Framemeister and then to my capture device (these days, almost always an
AverMedia Live Gamer Portable, which does 1080p 30 straight to an SD card
without the need for a PC). It's not a cheap solution by any means, but is
great for those of us with way too many vintage systems, and does resolve
all known issues.

I'm pretty sure the video anomalies are due to the capture device not interpreting the source video correctly, which can happen with "non-standard" signals from older hardware. For instance, with the Atari 2600, this can manifest itself as not capturing all of the ghosts in Pac-Man because of the technique used to display all of the ghosts in the game. It's quite common, actually.

I personally get around these legacy video issues for all eras of systems and all worldwide video formats by putting everything through an XRGB-mini Framemeister and then to my capture device (these days, almost always an AverMedia Live Gamer Portable, which does 1080p 30 straight to an SD card without the need for a PC). It's not a cheap solution by any means, but is great for those of us with way too many vintage systems, and does resolve all known issues.

14898:
The problem is that you’re running it thorough an emulator,  I’m using real Astrocade hardware, and the way I capture it, to a DVD recorder while simultaneously Y-ing with a powered splitter, it through a CRT TV gives you a game-accurate main feed (which is vital for light gun games) and a 480i accurate recording.   Alternately, I could use a Hauppauge Rocket without a computer, but I still need to demodulate the RF Video through a DVD recorder, which is way clearer than a VCR.

The only problem is that the Hauppauge digitizes the Light Gun Flash because it converts a lower definition progressive to either 480i or 480p, and most modern capture standards use a frame difference standard and a light gun flash ruins that effect.   But that has no impact on capturing the video game play to show the events of the game accurately.

Brian

14905:
I made a video for the 300-baud format, Bally BASIC game BANGMAN by Ernie Sams.  This program was published in the June 1979 issue of the Arcadian.

I decided to record this game because Paul and I will be discussing the June and July issues of the Arcadian in the upcoming Astrocast #6 podcast.  I figured that this  video would be a nice addition to the show notes.  This video was "captured" using a Canon Powershot SX60 HS.  The cool thing about that, compared to video capture cards, is that this is what you'd see if you loaded this game on your Astrocade.  Video capture cards show all of the Astrocade's overscans area-- which is actually a lot of extra screen area that a user never sees using real hardware and a TV.  Compared to yesterday's videos, I managed to reduce the moire effect (those wavy lines that run across the TV screen) by turning down the sharpness and contrast settings on the camera.

In this video, I show a 300-baud Bally BASIC "tape" (actually a WAV file) loading from my laptop computer.  I've never seen another video showing a 300-baud tape loading; I wonder if this is a first for YouTube?  I play BANGMAN and then I LIST the program (due, mainly, to Ronaldo's encouragement of this idea-- thanks!).  The video is about ten minutes long.  You can watch the video here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YjKWsy0Dbx8
[https://i.ytimg.com/vi/YjKWsy0Dbx8/hqdefault.jpg]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YjKWsy0Dbx8>

Bangman by Ernie Sams for Bally Arcade/Astrocade (Arcadian, June 1979)<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YjKWsy0Dbx8>
www.youtube.com
Game Instructions from Printing in ARCADIAN (1979): BANGMAN game program included this month is by Ernie Sams. It has a good scheme for entering characters w...

If you want to play this extremely exciting game, the you can download the original Bally BASIC version here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/Bangman%20(Ernie%20Sams).zip

Here are the BANGMAN instructions from the Arcadian.  These are combined from the original 1979 program listing and the later AstroBASIC version reprint in 1984 and well as the in-game instructions.

BANGMAN game program included this month is by Ernie Sams.  It has a good scheme for entering characters without their appearing on the screen, and a search routine can locate and account for multi-usage of a letter.  I am also including Ernie's sheet of documentation that will be a help to a lot of us.

BANGMAN is a take-off on the classic Hangman word spelling game.  It has two novel features - letters being entered are hidden from view of the opposing player - and the penalty for losing is not a hanging...

One person keys in a word to 10 letters; another tries to guess it with no more than 9 wrong guesses using the knob and trigger.

The program listing for BANGMAN is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_1/arcadian_vol_1_issue_07.pdf#page=2

This video is pretty clunky (i.e. it's not edited), but it gives a good example of what loading a program into Bally BASIC from the 300-baud interface is like.

Since I consider this my "first" video, please let me know what you think of it. Suggestions to make future videos better and ideas of what you'd like to see covered are most welcome!

14939:
John Mezzacappa wrote:

>>

I did not know that Robby Roto or any other game used the Astrocade Chipset. What other arcade games used this chipset?

>>


Between 1978 and 1985, there were six videogames released that used the Bally Arcade (Astrocade) chipset in hi-res mode.  Plus, there were a couple more that were electro-mechanical or not technically videogames (such as Professor Pac-Man, a trivia game).  More about all of these game can be read about in "Arcade Games Based Around Astrocade Chipset:"


http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/astrocade_arcade_games.txt


The earliest of the Astrocade chipset games (Seawolf II) is pretty basic (it's basically a 16K RAM, hi-res enabled Astrocade on one board), while later games added extras and used additional boards inside a "cage."  All of the released games can be emulated in MAME.  Even a prototype (Demons and Dragons) can be emulated, but the last time I checked that game, the sound didn't work.
