    John Mezzacappa wrote:>>I did not know that Robby Roto or any other game used the Astrocade Chipset. What other arcade games used this chipset?>>
Between 1978 and 1985, there were six videogames released that used the Bally Arcade (Astrocade) chipset in hi-res mode.  Plus, there were a couple more that were electro-mechanical or not technically videogames (such as Professor Pac-Man, a trivia game).  More about all of these game can be read about in "Arcade Games Based Around Astrocade Chipset:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/astrocade_arcade_games.txt
The earliest of the Astrocade chipset games (Seawolf II) is pretty basic (it's basically a 16K RAM, hi-res enabled Astrocade on one board), while later games added extras and used additional boards inside a "cage."  All of the released games can be emulated in MAME.  Even a prototype (Demons and Dragons) can be emulated, but the last time I checked that game, the sound didn't work.
Adam

The problem with copyrights is that they survive the original owner by 70 years! The only way to forgo that is for the original owner, in this case Bally, would have to release it. Astrovision only had a 5 year lease to use the arcade. After that it was to revert back to Bally. So the arcade is legally still a Bally product.Ken

    John Mezzacappa wrote:>>I did not know that Robby Roto or any other game used the Astrocade Chipset. What other arcade games used this chipset?>>
Between 1978 and 1985, there were six videogames released that used the Bally Arcade (Astrocade) chipset in hi-res mode.  Plus, there were a couple more that were electro-mechanical or not technically videogames (such as Professor Pac-Man, a trivia game).  More about all of these game can be read about in "Arcade Games Based Around Astrocade Chipset:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/astrocade_arcade_games.txt
The earliest of the Astrocade chipset games (Seawolf II) is pretty basic (it's basically a 16K RAM, hi-res enabled Astrocade on one board), while later games added extras and used additional boards inside a "cage."  All of the released games can be emulated in MAME.  Even a prototype (Demons and Dragons) can be emulated, but the last time I checked that game, the sound didn't work.
Adam

No, all the games are not released from copyright.  In fact, only a few cartridges are in the public domain.  Here is a mostly up-to-date list of the programs (carts and tapes) that are in the public domain for the Astrocade:

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/astrocade_pd_faq.txt

Michael has mentioned the portable Astrocade ("Retro Astro"), released in 2006.  You can read about that system here (make sure to read the entire article):

Ken mentioned that he thinks Bally owns the copyright to the Bally games, but I don't think that is correct.  I asked specifically about this question a couple of weeks ago.  Only Lance answered my query.  He said Warner Bros. probably owns the rights.

Adam

John Mezzacappa wrote:
>>
I did not know that Robby Roto or any other game used the Astrocade Chipset. What other arcade games used this chipset?
>>

Between 1978 and 1985, there were six videogames released that used the Bally Arcade (Astrocade) chipset in hi-res mode.  Plus, there were a couple more that were electro-mechanical or not technically videogames (such as Professor Pac-Man, a trivia game).  More about all of these game can be read about in "Arcade Games Based Around Astrocade Chipset:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/astrocade_arcade_games.txt

The earliest of the Astrocade chipset games (Seawolf II) is pretty basic (it's basically a 16K RAM, hi-res enabled Astrocade on one board), while later games added extras and used additional boards inside a "cage."  All of the released games can be emulated in MAME.  Even a prototype (Demons and Dragons) can be emulated, but the last time I checked that game, the sound didn't work.

Adam

14947:
I do work for AtGames (Atari Flashback 7, Sega Classic Console, Atari
Flashback Classics, etc.), and I can say that there is no interest in
something like that from a company that targets mainstream consumers. As a
point of comparison, we had trouble selling enough ColecoVision and
Intellivision Flashback consoles, so just imagine what a monumental dud an
Astrocade-based unit would be. If you're really interested in pulling
something like that off, it would have to come from some type of homebrew
effort. The potential audience is just not big enough.

What a lot of people do is come up with something based around something
like the Raspberry Pi. That's practical to pull off and can be adapted to
use original controllers, etc.

-Bill

 John Mezzacappa wrote:>>I did not know that Robby Roto or any other game used the Astrocade Chipset. What other arcade games used this chipset?>>
Between 1978 and 1985, there were six videogames released that used the Bally Arcade (Astrocade) chipset in hi-res mode.  Plus, there were a couple more that were electro-mechanical or not technically videogames (such as Professor Pac-Man, a trivia game).  More about all of these game can be read about in "Arcade Games Based Around Astrocade Chipset:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/astrocade_arcade_games.txt
The earliest of the Astrocade chipset games (Seawolf II) is pretty basic (it's basically a 16K RAM, hi-res enabled Astrocade on one board), while later games added extras and used additional boards inside a "cage."  All of the released games can be emulated in MAME.  Even a prototype (Demons and Dragons) can be emulated, but the last time I checked that game, the sound didn't work.

Well, technically all multicarts, or ROMS loaded on them for that matter, ROMs in general, etc., have always been a somewhat "grey" area.  So legally (depending on who is in power at the time) I can make a backup of software, movies etc. as long as I'm not bypassing any type of copy protection.  So if I legally own the ROM of a game then technically playing it on or loading it on a multicart is legal, as far as I understand it.  
So a multicart is not technically illegal, and certainly any ROM on it of a game you already own in that format on that system is "fine" to play, as well as any games released into the public domain.  For instance the entire library of Vectrex games from GCE were released into the public domain.  
As far as the NES "fiasco" as some are calling it, one simply has to know which stores are getting them and in what quantity.  As a Blu-ray steelbook collector I can tell you there are many sites where you can obtain this information, which I guess people outside of the steelbook collecting community may not be aware of (although many of these inventory sites were created by other collecting communities).  
On a side note I happen to like Galaga myself, and consider myself both an old school and modern gamer.  
-Michael

 John Mezzacappa wrote:>>I did not know that Robby Roto or any other game used the Astrocade Chipset. What other arcade games used this chipset?>>
Between 1978 and 1985, there were six videogames released that used the Bally Arcade (Astrocade) chipset in hi-res mode.  Plus, there were a couple more that were electro-mechanical or not technically videogames (such as Professor Pac-Man, a trivia game).  More about all of these game can be read about in "Arcade Games Based Around Astrocade Chipset:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/articles/astrocade_arcade_games.txt
The earliest of the Astrocade chipset games (Seawolf II) is pretty basic (it's basically a 16K RAM, hi-res enabled Astrocade on one board), while later games added extras and used additional boards inside a "cage."  All of the released games can be emulated in MAME.  Even a prototype (Demons and Dragons) can be emulated, but the last time I checked that game, the sound didn't work.
Adam

or RGB-modded console, you can also get your ColecoVision Flashback
upgraded by a gentleman on AtariAge who will essentially put a Raspberry Pi
inside with a decked out ColecoVision software build. He does the same for

To be frank, there is some type of multi-/flash-cart for almost every
classic videogame and computer system. To the letter of the law, very
little of it is legal (a few exceptions, like Vectrex multi-carts, are,
since most of that original library is actually in the public domain). For
all practical purposes, though, there is no longer the danger of commercial
harm, and most of this stuff is in very low volumes to tens of units to a
few thousand units (and the latter only when you're talking the upper
echelon of classic systems in terms of popularity).

Naturally, when you're talking about something commercial meant to sell in
the hundreds of thousands to millions of units like the NES Mini or Atari
Flashback Portable, then you obviously need to only deal in officially
licensed ROMs (and even then, a system like the Atari Flashback Portable
can still sport an SD card slot).

 John Mezzacappa wrote:>>I did not know that Robby Roto or any other game used the Astrocade Chipset. What other arcade games used this chipset?>>
Between 1978 and 1985, there were six videogames released that used the Bally Arcade (Astrocade) chipset in hi-res mode.  Plus, there were a couple more that were electro-mechanical or not technically videogames (such as Professor Pac-Man, a trivia game).  More about all of these game can be read about in "Arcade Games Based Around Astrocade Chipset:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/ball yalley/articles/astrocade_arca de_games.txt
The earliest of the Astrocade chipset games (Seawolf II) is pretty basic (it's basically a 16K RAM, hi-res enabled Astrocade on one board), while later games added extras and used additional boards inside a "cage."  All of the released games can be emulated in MAME.  Even a prototype (Demons and Dragons) can be emulated, but the last time I checked that game, the sound didn't work.

14958:
The single ROM is an 8K chip that replaced the need for the 4  2k chips. I is the better of the 2 different types. The 4 ROM system is not compatible with some of the cartridges out there. the 4 chip also can't be used to play any Blue Ram Basic programs because the text gets all screwed up. (read the Arcadian issues pertaining to the 3159 vs the 3164 chips). The 3 socketed chips may have come loose, but that is extremely rare. The 4 voltages that you can check 4 are +5V (check that on any small chip, the last pin when counting counter-clockwise from th "notch".  have your ground connection on the opposite corner, "kitty-corner". The RAM chips have 3 voltages going to them, Pin 1 (first from the "notch") is -5V, pin 8 is +12V, pin 9 is +5V and pin 16 is ground (0V reference). The 10V supply is best found on pin 40 of the center (custom address) socketed chip or pin 2 of the RF modulator (the large metal rectangular box plugged into the PCB header). If any of these voltages are off bu more than 10% you have a problem in that circuit.12V only goes to the RAM chips (those are the 8 located under the keypad that are in a pattern of 4 x 2). The -5 only goes to the Rams and the RF Modulator pin 8. On pin 5 of the modulator there should be 2.5V. If that is not there, your custom data chip is not working right. That doesn't necessarily mean it's bad, it could have one if it's signals coming in wrong.If you have access to an oscilloscope, and know how to use it, I could further walk you through some checks. Some, though, just defy trying to be fixed, and some are easy to find.Ken

So if someone can get someone of WB games (assuming they own the console rights) to write me to discuss if they want to make a Neo Astrocade, adding networking would be the incentive to push it over the top.

I have added the Bally Alley Astrocast podcast #6 today.

Episode 6 of the Bally Alley Astrocast covers The Incredible Wizard, the port of the arcade game Wizard of Wor.  Paul and I are joined by our new co-host Michael Di Salvo (yeah, Michael!).  Paul and I cover the Arcadian newsletter issues 7 and 8 (June and July 1979).  Paul and I discuss six letters to the Arcadian, dating from the Spring and Summer of 1979.  There is plenty of feedback and articles, plus Michael has a really cool segment with his son in which they review The Incredible Wizard together (this is one of my favorite parts of the episode).

The next Astrocast podcast (episode 7) will feature holiday feedback in the December episode.  If you have any holiday stories to share, then please send the feedback that you'd like to see included in episode 7 by December 16'th.  I can't wait to hear your tales!

You can download Astrocast #6 here:

http://www.ballyalleyastrocast.libsyn.com/rss


This episode is about three hours and fifteen minutes long.  Remember that you don't have to listen to it all in one sitting (the pause button is meant to be used at your discretion, as often as you like).


Special thanks to Chris for editing this podcast.  He took scattered segments, pieces, music, sound effects and made them into a complete final episode that works great as a whole.  Without his expertise, this episode wouldn't be nearly as fun-- and probably wouldn't exist at all.


Enjoy the podcast!


Adam

David Muncher has a fantastic history shrouded in mystery, suspense and a little bit of folklore.  
No seriously though, up until about 2004 this was I believe the only known release of this program, until I purchased a collection from a former Bally employee and came across two carts both with the name "Munchie" on the title menu. 
Both carts play the same and seem complete, but whether they are prototypes or just complete, unreleased games I cannot say. 
After a little digging on my part, some posts on this group, it turns out "Munchie" was in fact the name of the Pac-Man game Astrocade was going to release, its even advertised in a commercial:
Astrovision's Astro Professional Arcade commercial #2

|
|   |    |

   |

  |
|

Astrovision's Astro Professional Arcade commercial #2
 Astro Arcade, The Professional Videogame System that gives you four-player capability, three built-in games, a c...  |   |

  |

(Although at the time they were in transition and still going with the "Astro Arcade" console name). 

One of the software catalogs has it listed as well:
http://www.ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/bally/BPA_Catalog_(With_9_Games).pdf
Now how Pac-Man became Munchie and after the Atari lawsuit got "leaked" out and renamed and released as "Muncher" would be a great story unto itself (if it even happened that way or in that order).
I'm thinking we have the makings here for a future episode of the Bally Alley Astrocast:
"From Pac-Man to Munchie to Muncher: the untold story of how this maze game made it onto the Astrocade"
-Michael

I'm trying to configure the control setup for the Bally/Midway arcade prototype game Demons & Dragons that was created in about 1982.


I find Demons & Dragons intriguing because, although the game uses the Astrocade chipset, it seems to be able to use more than four colors on-screen at once.  There's nothing unusual about that really, as you can do that using the Astrocade by moving the left/right color boundary to get up to eight colors on-screen at time.  But this game seems to be using more colors than that.  Again, the Astrocade does have a palette of 256 colors and you can display more than eight colors on the screen at once using machine language interrupts, but this game doesn't seems to be using this trick.  Take a look and see for yourself.  How are there so colors on-screen at once?

MAME supports Demons & Dragons without sound, but other than that issue it seems to work okay.  I'm having problems trying to setup the game's unusual control scheme.  From what little I can find on the Internet, this game seems to be (sort of?) a twin-stick shooter that it setup like this:

14981:
From time to time, over the past decade or so (maybe even decades), I get interested in listening to 8-bit "chiptunes."  I listen to them mostly on YouTube.  I'm not prejudice: I don't care about the platform that makes the music.  The C64, the Atari 8-Bit home computers, the Amiga (yeah, baby!) and even the Spectrum have some incredible tunes available.  I like original electronic music (I'm not much into chiptunes that cover popular songs).  I'm always impressed by what some talented musicians are able to push out of the older computers (especially the Spectrum).


Each Astrocast podcast has been ending with music.  This has got me interested in Astrocade music again, especially modern music created on this "dead" platform.  The Astrocade is capable of some great sound effects, and there is even some pretty incredible music made on the platform.  However, unlike these previously mentioned systems, there isn't a modern Astrocade music scene.  I can understand this lack of music for the Astrocade.  For a start, there is a severe shortage of original Astrocade hardware.  However, the Astrocade emulator in MAME plays the sound effects and music pretty well.  So, I guess people could create music using the emulator, though it would require the music to be created as a cartridge (since, of course, you still can't save from either BASIC).


I'd be extremely interested to see what kind of music people can pump out of the Astrocade using modern programming methods and machine language.  From what little I understand about creating music on an 8-bit platform, I guess people use "trackers."  No such software exists for the Astrocade.  Is it possible to create it on an 8K cartridge and the Astrocade's 4K of RAM, or does such a program typically require more RAM?  Unlike "proper" computer systems, there would be no easy method to load music into the Astrocade... unless the 300-baud interface were used (but that would be a drag to use).   What alternative to load music into a cartridge might work for the Astrocade?


If an musicians out there in Bally/Astrocade-land would like to make some music on the Astrocade then it would be featured on an upcoming episode of the Astrocast podcast.


I haven't got an musical bones in my body... but I do love listening to music.  Am I the only person who would like to see the Astrocade sing again?


Adam

I first began listening to podcasts about a year and a half ago.  Chris, my former co-host, suggested The 2600 Game by Game Podcast.  I've still not caught up on all those episodes, but I'm getting close.  One of my favorite parts of any podcast, especially Ferg's podcast, are the Christmas/holiday memories that people share.  I've heard all sorts of great Atari holiday-related stories, but for some reason Ferg has been suppressing all the stories when people "boo" the Atari and are gung ho for the Bally.  It tell ya-- it's a conspiracy.  (Okay, it might be all in my head!)

I'm sure that there must be some Bally Arcade/Astrocade stories out there.  If you're one of those few people who got a Bally Arcade under the Christmas tree on Christmas Day, then I'd love to hear your story.  Maybe the Bally was your only system.  Or, perhaps you already had an Atari and you pitted the two systems against each other.  Maybe you got a Bally Arcade very early (in January 1978) before the Atari VCS was king of America's living rooms.  Or, maybe you got it as a gift while it was on clearance in 1984 for $25.  Do you have a sad tale to tell that involves asking for an Astrocade, but you got an Atari instead?  Were you were up all night crying about what might have been?  Possibly you have a four-player tale of playing 99 rounds of Checkmate against your parents and little sister on Christmas morning.

If your tale is holiday related (Christmas, Hanukkah, or whatever you celebrate), then I'd love to hear it!  Please write in (email the show) and tell us all about it.  If you're one of those awesome folks who likes to record audio feedback, then that's welcome too.

The next episode of the Astrocast will feature this holiday feedback in the December (okay, more like mid-January) episode.

I can't wait to hear your tales!

Adam

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_2/arcadian_vol_02_issue_09.pdfThe above link shows you how to build your own power supply transformer. It is relatively simple, as long as you know where the start and stop taps are.I do have one I could sell you. Because of it's rarity and the cost of buying the equivalent supply, the cost is going to be $50.00 plus P&H of $7.50. I could send it out as early as Jan. 3. It just plugs into the main PCB, no soldering required.
If you do build your own, it is advisable to either fuse each winding or put a switch on your primary winding(s). The )+5V bridge and lytic are ALWAYS ON regardless of the power switch on the Arcade. Ask my how I know!
If you have a short in the Arcade, the power supply can get extremely hot, causing it to melt! That may be why the transformer is not there.Do you have a voltmeter? If so, I can tell you where to test the voltages to see if there are any shorts.Ken

If your tale is holiday related (Christmas, Hanukkah, or whatever you celebrate), then I'd love to hear it!  Please write in (email the show) and tell us all about it.  If you're one of those awesome folks who likes to record audio feedback, then that's welcome too.

The next episode of the Astrocast will feature this holiday feedback in the December (okay, more like mid-January) episode.

I can't wait to hear your tales!

Adam
